extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers interested in life insurance practice and popular science (earth density)
extracted.subtask_description: An explanatory Popular Science Monthly magazine article aimed at general readers that (1) explains practical business, reserves, dividends, non-forfeiture and regulatory practices in life insurance, and (2) describes historical and experimental methods for determining the Earth's mean density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual premium components
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual premium may be looked upon as consisting of two parts, one defraying the annual cost of insurance dependent upon the death-rate, the other put aside as a reserve fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In earlier years the premium is larger than the actual cost of insurance and the over-payments are invested at compound interest to meet later deficiencies. The premium and reserve are adjusted to be equitable for the living as well as the dying at every year of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve (net valuation) per policy
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of every year an unexpended balance remains; dividing this by the number of survivors yields the amount that applies to each individual — called the net valuation or the reserve for each policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives tabular examples showing the reserve per policy by year and age; reserve values are computed from the working of premiums and death-claims (illustrative numeric examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve twofold function
rubrics_metrics.description: The reserve provides for the future and also annually reduces the amount at risk, whereby the cost of insurance becomes less than it would otherwise be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical examples show how an accumulated reserve reduces the insurer's amount at risk and lowers the cost-of-insurance portion of premiums in later years (examples for ages 45 and 94 given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation method — American net valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: The view of the reserve or net valuation presented is distinctively American and has been embodied in State legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other methods for determining the valuation take into account all future payments due and all losses and expenses to the end of the table; these alternative methods are acknowledged but not detailed in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loading — definition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: To the net premium a certain percentage is added to defray expenses and to provide for contingencies; it is called loading and together with the net premium constitutes the gross or office premium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mutual companies the loading is made higher than probable exigency to be safe; excess loading (over actual expenses) is one of the principal sources of dividends returned to policyholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of dividends and distribution method
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividends (sometimes called 'profits' or 'dividends') principally derive from the higher rate of interest realized than the legal standard assumes, from a lower mortality than the table estimates, and from the excess of loading over actual expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The universally adopted 'contribution plan' returns to every member precisely his proportion of the over-payments; the article provides a numeric illustration decomposing a cash dividend into contributing items (interest gain, excess loading, mortality savings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividend application options (cash or reversionary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most companies give policy-holders the option of either taking a cash return, or having the amount converted into a 'reversionary dividend,' payable with the policy (i.e., to purchase additional insurance by a single premium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An example shows converting a cash dividend into a net reversionary dividend supplying additional single-premium insurance (with deductions for management expenses); reversionary additions can form a very large item in old institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of lapsed/forfeited policies — general non-forfeiture practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies are made non-forfeitable after two or three annual payments, and when lapsed, if presented within reasonable time, either paid-up insurance is granted or a percentage of the reserve allowed as cash surrender value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some companies print fixed cash surrender values in the contract; actuaries have devised various formulas to determine strictly equitable surrender values that typically culminate in some percentage of the reserve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable surrender value principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrender values are adjusted so as to fully compensate the association for the loss of a withdrawing member while not confiscating the whole accumulated reserve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes a middle course between absolute forfeiture and full withdrawal of reserves — a percentage of reserve or paid-up insurance is generally allowed; illustrative statistics on company purchases of surrendered policies are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: New York non-forfeiture statute (Jan 1, 1880) — paid-up or single-premium conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: When a policy shall lapse for non-payment after being in force three years, the reserve and dividend additions on such policy shall, on demand within six months after such lapse, be taken as a single premium at the published rates of the company and be applied either to continue the policy in force at its full amount or to purchase paid-up insurance; provided the net value of the insurance given for such single premium shall in no case be less than two thirds of the entire reserve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory rule fixes a minimum conversion standard (net value at least two-thirds of reserve) and prescribes the conversion-to-single-premium mechanism for reinstatement/paid-up options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement and refund limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not correct that a company should be compelled to reinstate a lapsed policy without reexamination of the insured life, nor that the whole amount of premiums paid ought to be returned merely because no loss has occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such misconceptions are criticized as arising from a misunderstanding of insurance aims; companies must protect the pool and may require evidence on reinstatement; premiums are not automatically refundable in full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of cooperative/mutual-benefit life associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperative (mutual benefit) life associations based on collection of contributions on the death of members with no fixed premiums or adequate reserves are fundamentally impracticable and tend to fail as members age and healthy lives withdraw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains the mechanism of failure (initial apparent savings, later onerous contributions, healthy lives withdraw, preponderance of impaired lives), condemning such schemes as frauds or gross ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management standards: reserve interest assumption, investments, and surplus
rubrics_metrics.description: The accumulation of a reserve must earn at least the minimum rate of interest assumed as the basis of calculation; safe and profitable investments require exceptional skill, prudence, and forethought; companies keep surplus sufficiently high to meet legal standards (e.g., a 4% basis adopted by some States).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article warns that some funds remain unemployed reducing average interest; well-managed companies accumulate surplus over net reserve; failure of a life-insurance company traces to gross mismanagement or intentional fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: State supervision role
rubrics_metrics.description: State supervision should be limited to prescribing minimum reserves, the character of investments, and the publication of truthful statements of the condition of companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While state oversight has been beneficial, it cannot supplant individual judgment or probity; companies wishing to do business in states with specified reserve standards keep surplus to comply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitability principle of premium/reserve design
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual premium is a device to collect a larger amount than the death-rate in early years and to use these over-payments, improved at compound interest, to meet the deficiencies in later years; premiums and reserves are adjusted to be strictly equitable for the living as well as the dying at every year of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This summarizes the actuarial philosophy underlying level-premium whole-life insurance; numerical examples throughout the article illustrate the mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method — deflection of the plumb-line to determine Earth's mean density
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the deflection of the plumb-line caused by a nearby mountain by observing zenith-distances of a fixed star at two points (one near the mountain, one several miles away); calculate the mountain's mass / density and deduce the mean density of the earth from the ratio of attractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical limitations: the plumb-line diversion is minute and mountain mass/density/center-of-gravity estimates introduce errors; historical experiments (Maskelyne and Hutton at Shehallien) are discussed with their accuracy limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method — pendulum oscillations to determine Earth's mean density
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare durations of pendulum oscillations at different elevations or locations; differences between calculated and observed oscillation rates (accounting for elevation) indicate the attraction of nearby masses (mountains), from which Earth's mean density can be derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements include that the local surface be plane and form part of an exact sphere; nearby mountains disrupt results; historical uses and numeric outcomes (Carlini, Biot, Matthieu, Drobish) are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method — torsion balance to determine Earth's mean density
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a torsion balance (rod with masses suspended by a cord and a small mirror for angular measurement) to measure tiny attractive forces between known masses; these measurements can determine the Earth's mean density by comparing mountain/known-mass attractions to the Earth's attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes the torsion-balance apparatus and illustrates the method (figure referenced); the method is an alternative to plumb-line and pendulum approaches and avoids some estimation issues, though experimental detail is required for accuracy.
